about.title: Sine waves from a circle
about.math: x = cos t, y = sin t; y = A sin(ωx + φ); sin a + sin b = 2 cos((a − b)/2) sin((a + b)/2).
about.aha: Two nearly equal tones make a slow swelling (beats) at the difference of their frequencies: that is how musicians tune.
about.why: Every pure tone, alternating current, light and radio wave is A sin(ωt + φ).

about.title: Fourier series
about.math: square: (4/π) Σ sin((2k−1)x)/(2k−1); sawtooth: (2/π) Σ (−1)^(k+1) sin(kx)/k; triangle: (8/π²) Σ (−1)^(k+1) sin((2k−1)x)/(2k−1)².
about.aha: Jumps need terms that shrink only like 1/k and leave a 9% overshoot (Gibbs); corners need 1/k²; smooth curves need even faster decay.
about.why: MP3 and JPEG keep only the strongest Fourier terms; the timbre of an instrument is its list of harmonics.

about.title: Parametric and polar curves
about.math: Parametric: x = sin(at + φ), y = sin(bt). Polar: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ with r = cos kθ, 1 − sin θ, cθ.
about.aha: A rose r = cos kθ has 2k petals when k is even and k petals when k is odd (the odd one retraces itself after half a turn).
about.why: Oscilloscopes show Lissajous figures to compare two frequencies; cams and gears are cut from polar curves.

about.title: The number e
about.math: d/dx e^x = e^x; e = lim (1 + 1/n)^n; ln is the inverse of e^x; e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ.
about.aha: e is the only base whose curve has slope 1 at x = 0, so growth exactly proportional to size is always e^(kt).
about.why: Interest, populations, radioactive decay, cooling, charging capacitors and every damped vibration.

about.title: Chaos from a simple rule
about.math: xₙ₊₁ = r·xₙ(1 − xₙ): one value for r < 3, two above 3, four above 1 + √6 ≈ 3.449, chaos from r ≈ 3.5699 (each doubling 4.669 times sooner, Feigenbaum).
about.aha: Nothing random is in the rule, yet two starts 0.0001 apart soon disagree completely: sensitive dependence on initial conditions.
about.why: Population models, dripping taps, heart rhythms, weather forecasts.
